dedupe_keys.name: new york city inequities in emergency medical service response times 2010 to 2020

description: This case study examines whether emergency medical service (EMS) response times in New York City differ between neighbourhoods and what barriers explain the differences. The authors, researchers at George Washington University, the Georgia Institute of Technology and the University of Sydney, used open incident data from the Fire Department of the City of New York and regression analysis, and published the work in an open-access journal article. They analysed 15,349,368 EMS response times from 2010 to 2020 to measure disparities and 1,363,382 response times from 2020 to test candidate barriers. Coverage is the five boroughs of New York City at incident level. The article is free to read under a Creative Commons Attribution licence. Caveats: the study is observational, response time is only one measure of service quality, and the explanatory factors are area characteristics, not dispatch decisions. The study found significant inconsistencies in response times, with higher-risk areas more often failing to meet industry response standards. Simulation uses: a calibration and validation reference for ambulance location and dispatch models that include equity objectives, and a template for testing how station placement or demand growth changes neighbourhood response times. Related records: the FDNY EMS incident dispatch data (data-nyc-fdny-ems-incident-dispatch) is the kind of open data the study relies on, and the New York emergency service deserts study (case_study-nyc-emergency-service-deserts-access) looks at access in the same city.
